name: Wave 2 week 1: AI engineering, AWS, banking, fast local analytics

concepts.title: The AI engineer role and career path
concepts.kw: ai engineer role career path llm apps genai builder skills rag evals prompts apis portfolio job
concepts.s: AI engineers build products on top of existing models, mostly large language models, rather than training models from scratch. The job mixes software engineering, data work and careful evaluation.
concepts.d: A typical AI engineer connects an LLM to company data and tools: writing prompts, building retrieval (RAG) pipelines, calling functions and APIs, and shipping the result as a reliable feature. Unlike a machine learning engineer, who trains and deploys models, or a data scientist, who studies data to answer questions, the AI engineer treats the model as a component and spends most effort on data preparation, evaluation, latency, cost and safety. Core skills are Python, APIs, SQL, embeddings and vector search, prompt design, evaluation sets and monitoring. Data engineers and analysts move into the role well, because clean, well-organised data decides how good an LLM product is.
concepts.e: A support team wants answers drawn from 3,000 help articles. The AI engineer builds a pipeline that chunks and embeds the articles, retrieves the best matches for each question, asks the model to answer only from them, and tracks answer quality on 200 test questions.
concepts.c: How is an AI engineer's day-to-day work different from a machine learning engineer's?
concepts.i: Interviewers check that you treat LLMs as unreliable components: how you ground answers, evaluate them, control cost and latency, and handle failures. A small shipped project with an evaluation set beats a list of courses.

concepts.title: AWS data services map
concepts.kw: aws services map s3 glue athena emr kinesis msk lake formation dms step functions mwaa quicksight sagemaker data catalog lambda which service when
concepts.s: AWS has a service for almost every data job. Knowing which one handles storage, ingestion, processing, querying, orchestration and governance lets you sketch a platform quickly.
concepts.d: Storage sits in S3, usually as Parquet or an open table format such as Iceberg. The Glue Data Catalog holds table definitions that most services share. Ingestion uses DMS for database replication and change data capture, Kinesis or MSK (managed Kafka) for streams, and AppFlow or Lambda for SaaS and API sources. Processing runs on Glue jobs (serverless Spark), EMR (managed Spark and Hadoop clusters) or Lambda for small tasks. Athena runs serverless SQL over files in S3, and Redshift is the data warehouse. Step Functions or MWAA (managed Airflow) orchestrate pipelines, Lake Formation manages fine-grained access, QuickSight serves dashboards and SageMaker handles machine learning.
concepts.e: An e-commerce team replicates orders from Aurora with DMS into S3, cleans them with Glue jobs into Iceberg tables, lets analysts query them with Athena, loads curated marts into Redshift for dashboards, and runs it all on MWAA.
concepts.c: Which AWS services would you choose to replicate an operational database into a lake and query it with SQL?
concepts.i: Expect a whiteboard question: design a batch and streaming platform on AWS. Name the services, say why each was chosen, and mention the catalog, access control and cost.

concepts.title: Core banking data model
concepts.kw: core banking system cbs finacle flexcube bancs cif customer information file casa current savings accounts term deposits loans general ledger gl end of day eod batch
concepts.s: A core banking system (CBS) is the bank's system of record for customers, accounts, transactions and the general ledger. Most bank data work starts by understanding its data model.
concepts.d: Indian banks run platforms such as Finacle, Oracle Flexcube or TCS BaNCS. Each customer has a CIF (customer information file) record, linked to accounts: CASA (current and savings accounts), term deposits and loans. Every money movement posts transactions to accounts and, through product mappings, to general ledger (GL) heads, so account balances and the GL must always agree. Much processing happens in the end-of-day (EOD) batch: interest accrual, charges, standing instructions, loan dues and classification, and GL roll-ups. Data teams extract from CBS tables or reports into a warehouse for regulatory reporting, MIS and analytics, watching for back-dated entries, reversals and EOD timing.
concepts.e: A bank's MIS shows savings balances that differ from the GL by Rs 3.2 crore. The cause is a batch of back-dated reversals posted after the warehouse extract ran but before EOD closed.
concepts.c: Why must account balances and general ledger balances always agree, and what can make them drift in a data warehouse?
concepts.i: Banking interviews test whether you know CIF, CASA, GL and EOD, and how you would extract and reconcile core banking data without breaking the bank's batch window.

concepts.title: DuckDB and local-first analytics
concepts.kw: duckdb in process olap analytical database embedded sql parquet csv local laptop motherduck httpfs vectorised columnar single node
concepts.s: DuckDB is an analytical database that runs inside your program, like SQLite but built for analytics. It queries Parquet, CSV and JSON files with fast SQL on a single machine.
concepts.d: DuckDB needs no server: you open it from Python, R, the command line or even a browser, and query files directly, for example SELECT * FROM 'sales/*.parquet'. It stores and processes data in columns, executes queries in vectorised batches across all CPU cores, and can spill to disk when data is larger than memory. Extensions read from S3 and HTTP, Iceberg and Delta tables, and Postgres or MySQL databases. It is ideal for local analysis, testing transformations, small and medium pipelines, and CI checks. It is single-node, so very large or highly concurrent workloads still belong in a warehouse or Spark; MotherDuck offers a hosted version.
concepts.e: An analyst explores 40 GB of Parquet clickstream on a laptop with DuckDB in minutes, then the same SQL runs in CI to test the dbt model before it reaches the warehouse.
concepts.c: When would you choose DuckDB over a cloud warehouse, and when not?
concepts.i: Interviewers like hearing that you pick the smallest tool that works: DuckDB for single-node analysis and testing, a warehouse or Spark when data, concurrency or sharing outgrow one machine.

concepts.title: Vector databases and similarity search
concepts.kw: vector database similarity search ann index approximate nearest neighbour index hnsw ivf pgvector pinecone qdrant weaviate milvus vectorize metadata filtering
concepts.s: A vector database stores embeddings and quickly finds the items whose vectors are most similar to a query's. It is the retrieval engine behind most semantic search and RAG systems.
concepts.d: Text, images or products are turned into embeddings, lists of numbers where similar meaning means nearby vectors. Comparing a query against every vector is too slow at millions of items, so vector databases build approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes such as HNSW graphs or IVF clusters, trading a little recall for large speed gains. Options range from Postgres with the pgvector extension to dedicated stores such as Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus or Cloudflare Vectorize. Real systems also filter on metadata (tenant, date, language), combine vector and keyword search, and re-embed content when it changes. Measure recall against exact search, latency and cost.
concepts.e: A help-centre bot stores 50,000 article chunks in pgvector with an HNSW index. A question finds its 5 closest chunks in about 20 ms, filtered to the customer's product.
concepts.c: Why do vector databases use approximate rather than exact nearest neighbour search?
concepts.i: Expect to explain embeddings and ANN indexes, compare pgvector with a dedicated store, and say how you would measure retrieval quality.

concepts.title: Building a data lake on S3 with Lake Formation
concepts.kw: s3 data lake lake formation glue data catalog crawlers athena iceberg s3 tables lf tags permissions raw curated zones prefixes encryption
concepts.s: An S3 data lake stores files in zones on Amazon S3, describes them in the Glue Data Catalog, and uses Lake Formation to control who can see which databases, tables, columns and rows.
concepts.d: Data lands in a raw zone, is cleaned into a curated zone and modelled into a consumption zone, each a set of S3 prefixes or buckets, usually as Parquet or Apache Iceberg tables (S3 Tables offers managed Iceberg storage). Glue crawlers or pipeline code register tables in the Glue Data Catalog, so Athena, EMR, Glue and Redshift Spectrum all see the same definitions. Lake Formation then grants permissions on catalog resources, down to columns and rows, and LF-tags let you grant access by classification (for example pii=true) instead of table by table. Add encryption with KMS, S3 lifecycle rules for old raw data, and partitioning that matches query filters.
concepts.e: A bank keeps raw CBS extracts in a restricted bucket, curated Iceberg tables in another, and uses an LF-tag pii=true so analysts can query transactions while customer name and phone columns stay hidden.
concepts.c: Why use Lake Formation permissions instead of only S3 bucket policies?
concepts.i: Expect to lay out zones, the catalog and access control, explain how Athena and other engines share tables, and mention table formats, partitioning and cost.

concepts.title: Anti-money-laundering monitoring
concepts.kw: anti money laundering aml transaction monitoring structuring smurfing layering mule accounts str ctr fiu-ind pmla alerts case management false positives risk rating
concepts.s: Anti-money-laundering (AML) monitoring scans transactions for patterns that suggest money laundering, raises alerts for investigators, and supports reports to the regulator.
concepts.d: Banks risk-rate each customer from KYC data, then run transaction monitoring rules and models: structuring (many deposits just under a reporting threshold), rapid movement of funds in and out, sudden activity in dormant accounts, many small credits into one account (possible mule accounts), and links to high-risk counterparties. Alerts go to analysts in a case management system, who investigate, close or escalate them. In India, banks report to FIU-IND under the PMLA, including suspicious transaction reports (STRs) and cash transaction reports (CTRs). Most alerts are false positives, so tuning thresholds, segmenting customers and adding network analysis cut workload without missing real cases.
concepts.e: A rule flags an account receiving 45 UPI credits of Rs 9,000 to Rs 9,900 in two days, all moved out within hours. Graph analysis links it to 8 similar accounts, and the case leads to an STR.
concepts.c: Why do AML teams spend so much effort reducing false positives?
concepts.i: Senior banking interviews ask you to design transaction monitoring: rules versus models, customer risk, alert triage and case management, and how you would measure detection without drowning analysts.

concepts.title: Polars for fast DataFrames
concepts.kw: polars dataframe library rust apache arrow lazy api query optimisation expressions multithreaded streaming engine pandas alternative scan_parquet
concepts.s: Polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust on Apache Arrow. It is often many times faster than pandas because it uses all CPU cores and can optimise a whole query before running it.
concepts.d: Polars works with expressions such as pl.col("amount").sum().over("city"), which describe what to compute rather than looping over rows. Its lazy API (scan_parquet, then .collect()) builds a query plan first, so Polars can push filters down to the file reader, read only the needed columns, and combine steps. A streaming engine processes data in chunks when it doesn't fit in memory. There is no row index as in pandas, operations run in parallel by default, and data types are strict. It suits single-machine pipelines and feature engineering; for clusters you still need Spark, and many libraries still expect pandas, so conversion with to_pandas() is common.
concepts.e: A daily job that took 14 minutes in pandas to aggregate 60 million rows runs in under a minute after rewriting it with Polars' lazy API reading Parquet directly.
concepts.c: What does Polars' lazy API let the engine do that eager pandas code cannot?
concepts.i: Expect to compare Polars, pandas and Spark, explain lazy evaluation and expressions, and say when the switch is worth it.

concepts.title: Chunking documents for retrieval
concepts.kw: chunking strategies chunk size overlap recursive splitting semantic chunking headings parent child small to big documents rag retrieval tokens
concepts.s: Before documents can be searched in a RAG system they are split into chunks. Chunk size and boundaries decide whether retrieval finds the right passage with enough context.
concepts.d: Fixed-size chunking cuts text every few hundred tokens, usually with some overlap so ideas aren't split in half. Recursive or structure-aware splitting cuts at headings, paragraphs, then sentences, keeping sections intact. Semantic chunking starts a new chunk when the topic changes. Small chunks match questions precisely but lose context; large chunks keep context but blur the embedding and use more tokens. A common fix is small-to-big retrieval: search small chunks, then pass the larger parent section to the model. Keep metadata such as title, section, page and date with each chunk, handle tables separately, and test chunk settings against an evaluation set rather than guessing.
concepts.e: A policy manual split every 1,000 tokens returned half a table and the wrong exclusion clause. Splitting at headings into 300-token chunks with the section title attached raised correct retrievals on 150 test questions from 61% to 84%.
concepts.c: What goes wrong when chunks are too small, and when they are too large?
concepts.i: Interviewers ask how you chose chunk size and overlap, how you handle tables and headings, and how you proved the choice with retrieval metrics.

concepts.title: Amazon Redshift
concepts.kw: amazon redshift data warehouse mpp columnar ra3 managed storage serverless distribution style key even all sort keys copy spectrum concurrency scaling
concepts.s: Amazon Redshift is AWS's data warehouse: a columnar, massively parallel SQL database for analytics, available as provisioned clusters or Redshift Serverless.
concepts.d: Redshift stores tables in columns, compressed, and spreads rows across compute slices so queries run in parallel. RA3 nodes and Serverless separate compute from managed storage on S3. Table design matters: the distribution style (AUTO, KEY, EVEN or ALL) decides where rows live, and a good KEY on a common join column avoids moving data between nodes, while small dimensions can be copied to every node with ALL. Sort keys let queries skip blocks for filtered ranges. Load data in bulk with COPY from S3 rather than row inserts, query lake files with Redshift Spectrum, and use concurrency scaling or workload management for many users. Automatic table optimisation can choose keys for you.
concepts.e: Joining a 2-billion-row orders fact to customers was slow because rows were redistributed on every query. Distributing both tables on customer_id and sorting orders by order_date cut the dashboard query from 40 to 4 seconds.
concepts.c: Why does the choice of distribution key affect join speed in Redshift?
concepts.i: Expect questions on distribution and sort keys, loading with COPY, Serverless versus provisioned, and how Redshift compares with Snowflake or BigQuery.

questions.q: What does an AI engineer do, and how is the role different from a machine learning engineer?

p.t: Builds products on existing models such as LLMs
Grounds the model in company data with retrieval
Evaluates outputs with test sets and monitoring
ML engineers train and deploy models instead

questions.a: An AI engineer builds features on top of existing models, usually an LLM called through an API, instead of training new ones. Most of the work is grounding the model in company data with retrieval (RAG) using embeddings and a vector store, then proving it works with an evaluation test set and monitoring in production. A machine learning engineer focuses on training and deploying models from data.

questions.q: You are a data engineer who wants to move into AI engineering. What would you learn and build first?

p.t: Embeddings and vector search for retrieval
Prompting and structured outputs from LLM APIs
An evaluation set to measure answer quality
A small shipped project to show in a portfolio

questions.a: I would start with embeddings and vector search, since retrieval is where data engineering skills transfer directly. Then prompting and structured outputs from an LLM API, getting reliable JSON back. I would build an evaluation set of 100 or so test questions to measure accuracy before and after each change. Finally I would ship one small RAG project end to end and put it in my portfolio on GitHub with the evaluation results.

questions.q: Map the main AWS services to the stages of a data platform: storage, ingestion, processing, querying and orchestration.

p.t: S3 for storage with the Glue Data Catalog
DMS or Kinesis and MSK for ingestion
Glue jobs or EMR for processing
Athena or Redshift for querying
Step Functions or MWAA for orchestration

questions.a: Files live in S3, described in the Glue Data Catalog. Databases are replicated with DMS, streams arrive through Kinesis or MSK, and SaaS data through AppFlow. Processing runs on Glue jobs (serverless Spark) or EMR clusters, with Lambda for small steps. Analysts query the lake with Athena and the warehouse in Redshift, using Spectrum to reach lake files. Step Functions or MWAA (managed Airflow) orchestrate it all.

questions.q: When would you choose Glue jobs, EMR or Athena for a transformation on AWS?

p.t: Glue jobs for serverless Spark without managing clusters
EMR for large or long-running jobs needing tuning control
Athena for SQL transformations over S3 data
Cost depends on runtime and data scanned

questions.a: Glue jobs suit most pipelines: serverless Spark with no cluster to manage, paid per DPU-hour. EMR is better for very large or long-running jobs where I want control over tuning, instance types and spot capacity. Athena works well for SQL transformations over S3 data using CTAS or INSERT INTO, especially for lighter jobs. I compare cost too: Glue and EMR charge for runtime, Athena per TB of data scanned.

questions.q: Explain the core entities in a core banking system and how they relate.

p.t: CIF holds the customer record
Accounts such as CASA, deposits and loans link to the CIF
Transactions post to accounts and map to GL heads
End-of-day batch accrues interest and rolls up balances

questions.a: Each customer has a CIF record, the customer information file. Accounts link to the CIF: CASA (current and savings accounts), term deposits and loan accounts, and one customer can hold many. Every transaction posts to an account and, through product mappings, to general ledger heads, so account balances and the GL must agree. The end-of-day (EOD) batch then runs interest accrual, charges and loan dues, and rolls balances up to the GL.

questions.q: You need daily extracts from a bank's core banking system into a warehouse. What would you watch out for?

p.t: Run after the end-of-day batch closes
Handle back-dated entries and reversals
Reconcile totals to the general ledger
Protect customer PII and access

questions.a: I would schedule extracts after the end-of-day batch closes so I don't read half-posted data or slow the batch window. I would handle back-dated entries and reversals by loading on value date and reprocessing recent days. Every load would reconcile account totals with the general ledger using control totals. Customer PII from KYC data would be masked or encrypted, with strict access control in the warehouse.

questions.q: What is DuckDB and why has it become popular for data work?

p.t: Runs in-process with no server to manage
Queries Parquet and CSV files directly with SQL
Columnar, vectorised execution on all cores
Single-node, so not for huge shared workloads

questions.a: DuckDB is an analytical database that runs in-process, embedded in Python or the CLI with no server to manage. It queries Parquet, CSV and JSON files directly with SQL, so you can analyse a folder of files without loading them anywhere. Its columnar, vectorised engine uses every core, so it is very fast on a laptop. It is single-node, so huge datasets and many concurrent users still need a warehouse.

questions.q: How could DuckDB help a data team that runs dbt on a cloud warehouse?

p.t: Run tests and models locally or in CI cheaply
Work on samples of Parquet data
Avoid warehouse compute cost during development
Watch for SQL dialect differences

questions.a: DuckDB lets us run dbt models and tests locally and in CI on every pull request, using the dbt-duckdb adapter. We point it at samples or Parquet extracts as fixtures, so developers iterate quickly without burning warehouse compute cost or credits. The catch is SQL dialect differences between DuckDB and the warehouse, so we keep models to portable SQL or use macros, and still run a final check on the warehouse.

questions.q: How does a vector database find similar items quickly, and what do you give up?

p.t: Items are stored as embeddings
Approximate nearest neighbour indexes such as HNSW or IVF
Trades a little recall for speed
Similarity measured with cosine or dot product

questions.a: Each item is stored as an embedding vector. Instead of comparing the query with every vector, the database builds an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index such as an HNSW graph or IVF clusters, and only searches the promising region. Similarity is measured with cosine or dot product. The trade-off is recall: ANN may miss a few true neighbours that exact search would find, which you tune with index parameters.

questions.q: Would you use pgvector or a dedicated vector database for a new RAG product? How would you decide?

p.t: pgvector keeps vectors next to existing Postgres data
Dedicated stores for very large or demanding workloads
Metadata filtering and hybrid keyword search
Measure recall, latency and cost on real data

questions.a: With a few million vectors I would start with pgvector, which keeps vectors in the same Postgres database as the rest of our data, with joins and transactions. If we expect hundreds of millions of vectors or very high query rates, a dedicated store like Qdrant, Pinecone or Milvus makes sense. Either way I check metadata filtering per tenant and hybrid keyword search, then benchmark recall, latency and cost on our real data.

questions.q: How would you organise a data lake on S3 and control who can see what?

p.t: Raw, curated and consumption zones
Tables registered in the Glue Data Catalog
Lake Formation for table, column and row permissions
Open formats such as Parquet or Iceberg, partitioned

questions.a: I would split the lake into raw, curated and consumption zones in separate prefixes or buckets. Data is stored as Parquet or Iceberg tables, partitioned on common filters like date. Every table is registered in the Glue Data Catalog so Athena, EMR and Redshift Spectrum share definitions. Access goes through Lake Formation, with column-level and row-level permissions and LF-tags such as pii=true instead of per-bucket policies.

questions.q: Athena queries on your S3 lake are slow and expensive. What would you check?

p.t: Partitioning that matches query filters
Columnar formats and compression instead of CSV or JSON
Too many small files
Data scanned per query drives cost

questions.a: Athena charges by data scanned, so I would first look at bytes scanned per query. Then check that partitions match common filters so partition pruning works, and that data is stored as Parquet with compression rather than CSV or JSON. I would look for thousands of small files and compact them into files of a few hundred MB, for example with Iceberg's OPTIMIZE. Selecting only needed columns helps too.

questions.q: Describe how a bank's transaction monitoring for anti-money-laundering works.

p.t: Customers are risk-rated from KYC data
Rules and models detect suspicious patterns
Alerts are investigated in case management
Suspicious cases are reported, such as STRs to FIU-IND

questions.a: Each customer is risk-rated from KYC data and behaviour. Monitoring rules and models look for patterns like structuring just under thresholds, rapid movement of funds, dormant accounts waking up, or mule accounts receiving many small credits. Hits raise alerts that analysts triage and investigate in a case management system. Confirmed suspicious activity is reported, in India as an STR to FIU-IND under the PMLA.

questions.q: Your AML system raises 5,000 alerts a day and 98% are false positives. How would you improve it?

p.t: Segment customers so thresholds fit each group
Tune rules using outcomes of past alerts
Score and prioritise alerts with a model
Keep detection of true cases above a set level

questions.a: First I would segment customers into peer groups, so a trader's normal volumes don't trigger the same threshold as a student's. Then tune each rule using outcomes of past closed alerts to cut those that never lead to cases. A machine learning model can score alerts so analysts work the riskiest first. Throughout, I'd track detection rate on known true positives so we never trade missed cases for fewer alerts, and document it for the regulator.

questions.q: Why is Polars often faster than pandas?

p.t: Written in Rust on Apache Arrow memory
Runs operations in parallel on all cores
Lazy API optimises the whole query first
Expression-based instead of row loops and apply

questions.a: Polars is written in Rust and stores data in Apache Arrow columnar memory. It runs operations in parallel across all cores, while pandas mostly uses one. Its lazy API builds a query plan and optimises it first, with predicate and projection pushdown so it reads only needed rows and columns from Parquet. And code is written as expressions like pl.col("x").sum() instead of row loops or apply.

questions.q: Your pandas pipeline is slow on 80 million rows. Would you move it to Polars, DuckDB or Spark?

p.t: Polars or DuckDB if it fits one machine
Spark when data or work must spread across a cluster
Use lazy scans of Parquet with pushdown
Check library compatibility and rewrite cost

questions.a: 80 million rows usually fits one machine, so I would try Polars or DuckDB before Spark. Spark makes sense when data grows beyond a single machine or must run on a shared cluster. In Polars I would use lazy scan_parquet with filter and column pushdown instead of reading everything. I'd also check compatibility, since some downstream libraries need pandas, using to_pandas at the edges, and weigh the rewrite effort.

questions.q: How would you choose a chunking strategy for a RAG system over long policy documents?

p.t: Split on structure such as headings and paragraphs
Balance chunk size and overlap
Attach metadata like title, section and date
Compare settings on an evaluation set

questions.a: For policy documents I would split on structure, at headings, then paragraphs, using recursive splitting so sections stay whole. I'd start around 300 to 500 tokens per chunk with a small overlap, so clauses aren't cut. Each chunk carries metadata: document title, section name, page and effective date. Then I compare a few settings on an evaluation set of real test questions, measuring retrieval hit rate before picking one.

questions.q: Users say your RAG bot gives answers that miss context from the surrounding text. How would you fix retrieval?

p.t: Small-to-big or parent-document retrieval
Larger chunks or more overlap
Re-rank and retrieve more candidates
Measure with an evaluation set before and after

questions.a: I would switch to small-to-big retrieval: search small chunks for precision, then pass the parent section with the surrounding text to the model. I might also try larger chunks or more overlap where sections are long. Retrieving more candidates and using a re-ranker helps pick the best few. I'd measure each change on an evaluation set, before and after, checking retrieval hit rate and answer faithfulness.

questions.q: How do distribution styles and sort keys affect query speed in Redshift?

p.t: Distribution decides which node holds each row
KEY on join columns avoids redistributing data
ALL copies small dimensions to every node
Sort keys let queries skip blocks

questions.a: Distribution style decides which node and slice holds each row. With a KEY distribution on the join column, matching rows from both tables are co-located, so joins don't redistribute data over the network. Small dimension tables can use ALL, copying them to every node. Sort keys order data on disk, so range filters on, say, order date use zone maps to skip blocks that can't match.

questions.q: When would you pick Redshift Serverless over a provisioned cluster, and how does Redshift compare with Snowflake?

p.t: Serverless for spiky or unpredictable workloads
Provisioned for steady heavy use with reserved pricing
Snowflake separates compute warehouses per workload
Consider ecosystem fit and data sharing

questions.a: Redshift Serverless suits spiky or unpredictable workloads, since you pay per use in RPU-hours and it scales automatically. A provisioned RA3 cluster with reserved pricing is cheaper for steady, heavy use. Snowflake gives each workload its own virtual warehouse with separate compute, which is simpler for isolation. I'd also weigh ecosystem fit: Redshift integrates tightly with AWS, while Snowflake runs multi-cloud and has strong data sharing.
